---
title: "Glossary"
---

A running glossary of the genetics, database and statistics terms used in this course. Definitions are kept short, and each one links to the unit where the term is introduced.

## Part 1: Mendelian genetics

### Genes and genomes

**Allele**: one version of a gene. Alleles differ in DNA sequence. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**C-value paradox**: genome size does not follow gene number or organism complexity, because most of a large genome is non-coding DNA. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Cytogenetic band**: a chromosome address such as 11p15.4: chromosome, arm, region, band and sub-band, numbered outwards from the centromere. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Dominant / recessive**: if *Aa* has the same phenotype as *AA*, then *A* is dominant and *a* is recessive, for that phenotype. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Gene**: a DNA segment that carries the information for one functional product, usually a protein. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Gene tree**: a tree of genes in which speciation nodes define orthologs and duplication nodes define paralogs. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Genotype**: the alleles an individual carries at a locus, e.g. *Aa*. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Hemizygous**: having only one copy of a gene, as males do for genes on the X chromosome. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Homozygous / heterozygous**: carrying two identical alleles, or two different alleles, at a locus. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Locus**: the position of a gene on a chromosome. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Model organism**: a species that is easy to grow and cross, used because many of its genes are shared with other species. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Ortholog**: genes in different species that descend from one gene in their common ancestor. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Paralog**: genes related by a duplication within one genome. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Phenotype**: an observable or measurable trait, from a disease to a protein band on a gel. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Wild type**: the standard allele or phenotype in a lab population, written with a +, e.g. *w*^+^. See [Genetics as information](intro-genetics/lec.qmd).

### Mendel's crosses

**Branch-line (forked-line) method**: solving a multi-gene cross one gene at a time, then multiplying the probabilities along each branch. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Dihybrid cross**: a cross between individuals heterozygous for two genes (*AaBb* × *AaBb*). It gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotypes when the genes are unlinked. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Law of independent assortment**: alleles of different genes enter gametes independently, because homologue pairs orient independently at metaphase I. It holds for unlinked genes. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Law of segregation**: the two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes, ½ each, because homologues separate in meiosis I. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Monohybrid cross**: a cross between individuals heterozygous for one gene (*Aa* × *Aa*). It gives 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes and 3 : 1 phenotypes. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Punnett square**: a grid of one parent's gametes against the other parent's gametes. Each cell is one equally likely fertilisation. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Reciprocal cross**: the same cross done both ways round, to test whether it matters which parent carries the allele. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**Testcross**: a cross to a homozygous recessive individual. The offspring phenotypes show the other parent's gametes directly. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

**True-breeding line**: a line that gives only offspring like itself when self-fertilised, because it is homozygous. See [Mendel](mendel/lec.qmd).

### Probability and the χ² test

**Binomial distribution**: the probability of k outcomes of one kind in n independent trials, (n choose k) pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. It is used for family composition. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**χ² goodness-of-fit test**: a test of whether observed counts fit the counts expected from a hypothesised ratio, using χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Conditional probability**: the probability of an event given that another event is known to have happened. For example, P(carrier | unaffected child of *Aa* × *Aa*) = 2/3. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Critical value**: the χ² value that is exceeded with probability 0.05 under H0 (3.84 for df = 1). See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Degrees of freedom (df)**: the number of counts that are free to vary once the total is fixed. It is k − 1 for k classes and a ratio given in advance. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Fail to reject**: the outcome when p ≥ 0.05. The data are consistent with H0, but this does not prove H0. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Null hypothesis (H0)**: the hypothesis being tested, here a Mendelian ratio such as 3:1. Expected counts are computed assuming it is true. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**p-value**: the probability, if H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that H0 is true. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Product rule**: the probability that independent events all happen is the product of their probabilities, e.g. P(*aabbcc*) = (¼)³. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

**Sum rule**: the probability that one of several mutually exclusive events happens is the sum of their probabilities. See [Probability & the χ² test](probability-chisq/lec.qmd).

### Extensions to Mendel

**Allelic series**: several alleles of one gene in a dominance hierarchy, e.g. *C* > *c^ch^* > *c^h^* > *c*. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Codominance**: the heterozygote shows the phenotypes of both alleles in full, as in blood type AB (*I^A^I^B^*). See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Complementary genes**: two genes that are both needed for a phenotype, giving a 9 : 7 F₂ ratio. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Dominant negative**: a mutant protein that interferes with the normal protein from the other allele, for example in a dimer. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Duplicate genes**: two redundant genes, where one working copy of either is enough, giving a 15 : 1 F₂ ratio. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Epistasis**: the genotype at one gene hides the effect of another gene. This changes the dihybrid 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio into ratios such as 9 : 3 : 4 or 9 : 7. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Expressivity**: how strongly a phenotype shows in the individuals who have it. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Haploinsufficiency**: one working copy of a gene does not make enough product for a normal phenotype, so a loss-of-function allele is dominant. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Haplosufficient**: a gene for which one working copy gives a normal phenotype. This is why most loss-of-function alleles are recessive. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Hypostatic**: describes a gene whose effect is hidden by an epistatic gene. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Incomplete dominance**: the heterozygote's phenotype lies between those of the two homozygotes, so the F₂ phenotypes are 1 : 2 : 1, as in snapdragon flower colour. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Multiple alleles**: more than two alleles of a gene exist in a population, as in the ABO blood group. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Penetrance**: the fraction of individuals with a given genotype who show the expected phenotype at all. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Pleiotropy**: one gene or allele affecting several different traits. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

**Recessive lethal allele**: an allele that kills homozygotes. Among the survivors of a heterozygote cross this gives a 2 : 1 ratio, as for the yellow mouse allele *A^Y^*. See [Extensions to Mendel](mendel-extensions/lec.qmd).

### Pedigrees

**Ascertainment bias**: distortion of observed ratios caused by the way families are found, for example only through an affected child. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Consanguinity**: a mating between related people, drawn as a double line. It raises the risk of recessive disease. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Male-to-male transmission**: a trait passed from father to son. It rules out X-linked dominant inheritance and makes X-linked recessive inheritance unlikely. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Obligate carrier**: an unaffected person who must be heterozygous because of where they are in the pedigree, for example a parent of a child with a recessive disease. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Pedigree**: a family tree drawn with standard symbols that shows who is affected by a trait and how they are related. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Sib method**: a correction for ascertainment bias that counts the affected siblings of each affected child in turn. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**Proband**: the affected person through whom a family first comes to attention, marked with an arrow. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

### Databases

**ClinVar**: the NCBI database that links human variants to clinical interpretations. Each record has a classification and a review status. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**HGVS notation**: the standard naming of variants, e.g. `c.1222C>T` (coding DNA) and `p.Arg408Trp` (protein). See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

**MIM number**: the six-digit identifier of a gene or disease entry in OMIM. See [Pedigree analysis](pedigrees/lec.qmd).

## Part 2: Chromosomes and mapping

### Chromosome theory and sex linkage

**Bivalent**: a pair of synapsed homologues in prophase I, with four chromatids in all. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Chromosome theory of inheritance**: genes are carried on chromosomes, and the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis explains Mendel's laws. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Criss-cross inheritance**: an X-linked recessive trait passes from mother to sons and from father to daughters, so reciprocal crosses give different results. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Dosage compensation**: mechanisms that equalise X-linked gene expression between XX and XY individuals, such as X inactivation. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Haplodiploidy**: sex determination in which males develop from unfertilised eggs and are haploid, as in bees, ants and wasps. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Heterogametic sex**: the sex with two different sex chromosomes (XY males, ZW females), which therefore makes two kinds of gamete. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Homologous chromosomes**: the two copies of a chromosome in a diploid cell, one from each parent, with the same genes in the same order. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Nondisjunction**: homologues (in meiosis I) or sister chromatids (in meiosis II) fail to separate, giving n + 1 and n − 1 gametes. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Reductional / equational division**: meiosis I separates homologues (2n → n); meiosis II separates sister chromatids. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Sister chromatids**: the two identical DNA copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

**Z-linkage**: inheritance of genes on the bird Z chromosome. Hens (ZW) are hemizygous. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

***SRY***: the Y-linked gene (Yp11.2) encoding the testis-determining factor, which switches on male development in mammals. See [Chromosome theory & sex linkage](chromosome-theory/lec.qmd).

### Linkage and recombination

**Centimorgan (cM, map unit)**: the distance with on average one crossover per 100 chromatids. It is about 1% RF for short intervals. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Coupling (cis) / repulsion (trans)**: the linkage phase. In *A B* / *a b* the dominant alleles are on one homologue; in *A b* / *a B* there is one on each. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Crossing over / chiasma**: reciprocal exchange between non-sister chromatids in prophase I. A chiasma is where it is seen under the microscope. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Four-strand stage**: crossing over happens after replication, so one crossover makes only 2 of the 4 meiotic products recombinant. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Haldane map function**: RF = ½(1 − e^−2d^). It assumes crossovers occur independently. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Kosambi map function**: RF = ½ tanh(2d). It allows for interference. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Linkage**: the tendency of genes close together on one chromosome to be inherited together, giving an excess of parental combinations (RF < 0.5). See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Map function**: a formula that converts between map distance and RF, correcting for hidden multiple crossovers. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Parental / recombinant class**: offspring with the allele combinations the heterozygous parent received from its own parents, or with new combinations made by crossing over. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Poisson model of crossing over**: the assumption that crossovers occur independently, so that the number of crossovers on a chromatid is Poisson-distributed with mean *d*. It underlies Haldane's map function. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

**Recombination frequency (RF)**: recombinant offspring divided by all offspring. It lies between 0 and 0.5. See [Linkage & recombination](linkage/lec.qmd).

### Three-point crosses

**Coefficient of coincidence (CoC)**: observed double crossovers divided by expected double crossovers. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Double crossover (DCO)**: a chromatid with one crossover in each of two adjacent intervals. It moves only the middle gene to the other homologue. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Expected double crossovers**: RF~I~ × RF~II~ × N, the number expected if crossovers in the two intervals are independent. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Gene order (from a three-point cross)**: the middle gene is the one that differs between the double crossover classes and the parental classes. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Interference (I)**: I = 1 − CoC. Positive interference means that one crossover makes another one nearby less likely. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Negative interference**: CoC > 1, i.e. more double crossovers than expected. It is rare; in a hand calculation it usually means the gene order is wrong. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Reciprocal classes**: two offspring classes with opposite alleles at every locus. They are made by the same crossover event, so they are similar in number. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Single crossover (SCO)**: a chromatid with one crossover, in one of the two intervals of a three-point cross. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

**Three-point testcross**: a cross of an individual heterozygous for three linked genes to a triple recessive tester. The 8 offspring classes show the 8 gamete types. See [Three-point crosses](three-point-cross/lec.qmd).

### Human linkage and LOD scores

**DNA marker**: a site in the DNA where people differ (RFLP, microsatellite, SNP), used to tell a parent's two homologues apart. It need not affect the phenotype. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**Exclusion mapping**: using LOD ≤ −2 to rule out that a gene lies within a given distance of a marker. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**Informative meiosis**: a meiosis in which the parent is heterozygous at both the disease locus and the marker, so each child can be scored as recombinant or non-recombinant. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**Likelihood**: the probability of the observed data, read as a function of a parameter. For a phase-known family, L(θ) = θ^k^(1 − θ)^n−k^. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**Linkage phase (in a pedigree)**: which marker allele lies on the same homologue as the disease allele. It can be known from the grandparents; otherwise both phases are averaged with probability ½ each. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**LOD score**: log~10~ of the likelihood ratio L(θ)/L(0.5), comparing linkage at θ with no linkage. LODs from independent families add. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**LOD threshold**: LOD ≥ 3 is accepted as linkage, LOD ≤ −2 excludes linkage at that θ, and values in between are inconclusive. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**Microsatellite**: a short tandem repeat such as (CA)~n~, with many length alleles, so most people are heterozygous. It is typed by PCR. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

**θ̂ (maximum likelihood estimate)**: the θ at which the LOD curve peaks. For phase-known families it equals total recombinants divided by total meioses. See [Human linkage & LOD scores](lod-scores/lec.qmd).

## Part 3: DNA, mutation and gene function

### DNA structure and replication

**+ strand / − strand**: the two strands of a reference chromosome. Databases such as dbSNP report alleles on the + strand, while c. names use the gene's own coding strand. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

**Antiparallel**: the two strands of a double helix run in opposite directions, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

**Gene conversion**: non-reciprocal transfer of sequence, caused by mismatch repair of heteroduplex DNA. It gives 3 : 1 instead of 2 : 2 in a tetrad. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

**Holliday junction**: a point where strands cross between two homologous DNA helices during recombination. Cutting it gives a crossover or a non-crossover. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

**Reverse complement**: the partner strand of a sequence, written 5′→3′: complement every base, then reverse the order. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

**Semiconservative replication**: each daughter helix has one old and one new strand, as Meselson and Stahl showed. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

**Transformation**: a heritable change caused by DNA taken up from outside the cell, as found by Griffith and by Avery. See [DNA structure & replication](dna-recap/lec.qmd).

### Mutation and complementation

**Ames test**: a test for mutagens that counts *his*⁻ → *his*⁺ reversions in *Salmonella*, with liver extract added. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Cis–trans test**: comparing two recessive mutations on different homologues (*trans*) with both on one homologue (*cis*). If *trans* is mutant and *cis* is wild type, the mutations are in the same gene. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Cistron**: Benzer's name for the unit of function defined by the cis–trans test; today, a gene. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Complementation group**: a set of mutations that fail to complement each other, which is one gene. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Complementation test**: cross two recessive mutants. A wild-type F₁ means the mutations are in different genes; a mutant F₁ means they are in the same gene. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Fluctuation test**: parallel cultures show jackpots (variance much larger than the mean). This shows that mutations arise at random, before selection. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Loss / gain of function**: an allele that reduces or removes a gene's activity, or one that raises it or adds a new activity. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Minimal medium / complete medium**: the simplest medium on which the wild type grows, versus a medium supplemented with amino acids and vitamins, on which auxotrophs also grow. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Mutagen**: an agent that raises the mutation rate above the spontaneous rate. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift**: a point mutation that keeps the amino acid, changes it, or creates a stop codon; or an insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

**Transition / transversion**: a substitution within a base class (A↔G, C↔T), or one between a purine and a pyrimidine. See [Mutation & complementation](mutation/lec.qmd).

### Gene expression

**Alternative splicing**: one gene gives several mRNAs by including or skipping exons. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**Intronic HGVS position (c.92+1, c.93-21)**: a base in an intron, counted from the nearest exon base: +*n* after the end of an exon, −*n* before the start of the next one. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

***rII* mutant**: a phage T4 mutant that makes plaques on *E. coli* B but not on K12(λ), so that rare wild-type phage can be selected. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**Intragenic suppression**: a second mutation in the same gene restores function, for example a (−) frameshift next to a (+) frameshift. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**Isoform**: one of several proteins made from the same gene. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**MANE Select**: the one default transcript per gene agreed by NCBI and Ensembl. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)**: destruction of an mRNA with a premature stop codon. Such alleles therefore usually act as nulls. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**Reading frame**: the grouping of a sequence into consecutive codons, starting from the start codon. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

**Splice donor / acceptor**: the GU at the 5′ end and the AG at the 3′ end of an intron. See [Gene expression](gene-expression-recap/lec.qmd).

## Part 4: Genome analysis

### Digital analysis of DNA

**Cloning vector**: a small DNA molecule, such as a plasmid, with an origin of replication, a selectable marker and cloning sites. It is used to copy a DNA fragment in bacteria. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Coverage**: the average number of sequencing reads covering each base: number of reads × read length / genome length. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Ct (threshold cycle)**: the PCR cycle at which the product crosses a detection threshold. With 10× more template it is crossed about 3.3 cycles earlier. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Gel electrophoresis**: separation of DNA fragments by size in an agarose gel. The distance run falls roughly linearly with log(size). See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Partial digest**: a digest in which some sites were not cut. It gives extra, larger fragments that are sums of neighbouring fragments. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**PCR (polymerase chain reaction)**: repeated cycles of denaturing, annealing and extension that copy the DNA between two primers exponentially. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Primer-dimer**: a short PCR artefact, made when two primers anneal to each other and are extended. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Restriction enzyme**: a bacterial enzyme that cuts double-stranded DNA at a specific short recognition site, usually a palindrome. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Reverse primer**: the PCR primer that pairs with the top strand. Its sequence is the reverse complement of the end of the target region. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**RFLP**: a restriction fragment length polymorphism, a variant that creates or destroys a restriction site and so changes fragment sizes. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Sanger sequencing**: chain-termination sequencing with dye-labelled dideoxynucleotides. The products are sorted by length to read the bases. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Sticky end**: a short single-stranded overhang left by a staggered cut. It can pair with any end cut by the same enzyme. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

**Supercoiled DNA**: the twisted, compact form of an uncut circular plasmid. It runs faster on a gel than the same DNA when linear. See [Digital analysis of DNA](digital-dna/lec.qmd).

### Genome annotation

**Annotation**: the evidence-based, versioned description of where the genes and other features lie in a genome and what they do. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Bit score**: a normalised alignment score. Each extra bit halves the E-value. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**BLAST**: a program that finds local sequence similarity by seeding short word matches and extending them (blastn, blastp, blastx, tblastn). See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Contig**: a continuous stretch of sequence assembled from overlapping reads. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**E-value**: the number of alignments at least this good expected by chance in a database of this size. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Genome browser**: a tool, such as UCSC or Ensembl, that shows annotation tracks along chromosome coordinates. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Open reading frame (ORF)**: a stretch from a start codon to the next in-frame stop codon. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Pseudogene**: a gene copy that can no longer make a working product. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Substitution matrix (BLOSUM62)**: a table of scores for aligning each pair of amino acids, positive for identical or similar residues. See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

**Untranslated region (UTR)**: the part of an mRNA before the start codon (5′ UTR) or after the stop codon (3′ UTR). See [Genome annotation](genome-annotation/lec.qmd).

### Genomic variation

**Allele number (AN)**: the number of chromosomes typed at a site. Allele frequency = allele count / AN. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**Balanced polymorphism (heterozygote advantage)**: a polymorphism kept in a population because heterozygotes are the fittest, as for HbS where malaria is common. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**Copy-number variant (CNV)**: a segment, from a kilobase to several megabases long, present in different numbers of copies in different people. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**gnomAD**: a large database of allele frequencies from exomes and genomes, grouped by genetic ancestry. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**Haplotype**: the set of alleles carried on one chromosome. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**Indel**: a small insertion or deletion of bases. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**Lactase persistence**: continued lactase production in adults. In Europeans it is mainly due to the dominant *LCT* −13910T allele (rs4988235). See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**Linkage disequilibrium (LD)**: a non-random association of alleles at nearby sites in a population. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**r² and D′**: scaled measures of linkage disequilibrium between 0 and 1, shown in genome browsers. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**rs number**: the stable dbSNP identifier of a variant position. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

**SNP**: a single-nucleotide variant common enough to count as a polymorphism. See [Genomic variation](genomic-variation/lec.qmd).

## Part 5: Chromosomes in detail

### The eukaryotic chromosome

**Breakage–fusion–bridge cycle**: broken sister chromatids fuse into a dicentric chromosome, which breaks again at anaphase, over and over. It gives duplications and deletions. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Centromere**: the site on a chromosome where the kinetochore assembles. In humans it is Mb-long α-satellite arrays marked by the histone variant CENP-A. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**End-replication problem**: the last primer on the lagging strand cannot be replaced by DNA, so linear chromosomes shorten at each replication. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Heterochromatin**: compact, gene-poor, late-replicating chromatin. It is built largely on satellite repeats (constitutive), or silenced in some cells only (facultative, e.g. the inactive X). See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Karyotype**: the full chromosome set of a cell, ordered by size, centromere position and banding, and written e.g. 47,XY,+21. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Nucleosome**: 147 bp of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. There is about one per 200 bp of chromatin. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Position-effect variegation**: mosaic silencing of a gene that has been moved next to heterochromatin. The heterochromatin spreads into the gene in some cells but not others. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Telomerase**: a reverse transcriptase (TERT protein plus the TERC RNA template) that adds telomere repeats to chromosome ends. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Telomere**: the end of a linear chromosome. In vertebrates it is TTAGGG repeats with a 3′ overhang and the shelterin proteins, which hide the end from DNA repair. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

**Yeast artificial chromosome (YAC)**: a vector with an origin (ARS), a centromere (CEN) and two telomeres. It carries 100 kb to over 1 Mb of foreign DNA in yeast. See [The eukaryotic chromosome](eukaryotic-chromosome/lec.qmd).

### Rearrangements and aneuploidy

**Allopolyploid / autopolyploid**: a polyploid whose chromosome sets come from different species / from one species. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Alternate / adjacent segregation**: the ways the four chromosomes of a reciprocal translocation carrier can go to the poles. Only alternate segregation gives balanced gametes. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Inversion loop**: the loop that the homologues of an inversion heterozygote form so they can pair gene by gene. Crossovers inside the loop give unbalanced products. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Maternal age effect**: the steep rise in trisomy risk with the mother's age. It is caused mainly by meiosis I errors in oocytes that have been arrested for a long time. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR)**: crossing over between mispaired low-copy repeats. It gives recurrent deletions and duplications of the segment between them. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Paracentric / pericentric inversion**: an inverted segment that excludes / includes the centromere. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Philadelphia chromosome**: der(22) of t(9;22). It carries the *BCR*::*ABL1* fusion gene in chronic myeloid leukaemia. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Polytene chromosome**: a giant chromosome made of many aligned copies, with visible bands. It is used for deletion mapping in *Drosophila*. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Pseudodominance**: a recessive allele is expressed in a heterozygote because a deletion has removed the other copy. It is used for deletion mapping. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Quadrivalent**: the cross-shaped pairing of the four chromosomes of a reciprocal translocation carrier at meiosis I. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

**Robertsonian translocation**: a fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes near their centromeres. Carriers have 45 chromosomes. See [Rearrangements & aneuploidy](rearrangements-aneuploidy/lec.qmd).

### Bacterial genetics

**Auxotroph**: a mutant that cannot make a nutrient, so it grows only if the medium supplies it (e.g. Trp⁻). The wild type, which grows on minimal medium, is a prototroph. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Cotransduction frequency**: the fraction of transductants, selected for one donor marker, that also received a second marker. The higher it is, the closer the genes. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**F′ factor**: an F plasmid that carries a piece of the bacterial chromosome. It makes the recipient a partial diploid (merodiploid). See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Generalized transduction**: transfer of a random piece of bacterial DNA from one cell to another inside a phage head (e.g. P1, about 100 kb). See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Hfr strain**: a bacterial strain with the F factor integrated into its chromosome, so that it transfers chromosomal genes in a fixed order from oriT. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Interrupted mating**: breaking Hfr × F⁻ pairs apart at set times to measure each marker's time of entry. This gives a map in minutes. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Map minute**: the *E. coli* map unit. 100 minutes ≈ the whole 4.64 Mb chromosome, so 1 minute ≈ 46 kb. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Time of entry**: the minute at which a donor marker first enters the recipient in interrupted mating. It is found by extrapolating the rise in recombinants back to zero. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

**Replica plating**: printing the colonies of a master plate onto several test plates with a velvet, to score many colonies for growth at once. See [Bacterial genetics](bacterial-genetics-recap/lec.qmd).

### Organelle inheritance

**Endosymbiosis**: the origin of mitochondria from an alphaproteobacterium, and of chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium, taken up by a host cell. Most of their genes were later transferred to the nucleus. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Heteroplasmy**: both normal and mutant copies of the mitochondrial (or chloroplast) genome in one cell or person. The heteroplasmy level is the fraction of mutant copies. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Homoplasmy**: all copies of the organelle genome in a cell or person are identical (a level of 0% or 100%). See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Maternal inheritance**: organelle genomes pass from the mother only, with the egg cytoplasm. Reciprocal crosses therefore differ, and fathers do not transmit. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**MELAS**: mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes. It is usually caused by heteroplasmic m.3243A>G in *MT-TL1* (tRNA-Leu). See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Mitochondrial bottleneck**: each oocyte is founded by a small number of mtDNA copies before they are amplified. Offspring heteroplasmy therefore varies widely around the mother's level (variance h(1−h)/N). See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Mitochondrial donation**: transfer of the mother's nuclear DNA (spindle or pronuclei) into an enucleated donor egg or zygote, so that the child has the donor's mtDNA. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Ragged red fibres**: muscle fibres with clumped, abnormal mitochondria that stain red with Gomori trichrome. They are a sign of mitochondrial myopathy. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Replicative segregation**: random sorting of organelle genomes between daughter cells at division. It changes heteroplasmy between tissues and over time, and causes variegation in plants. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Threshold effect**: symptoms of a mtDNA disease appear only when the mutant fraction in a tissue exceeds a level that depends on the tissue and the variant, often 60–90%. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

**Uniparental inheritance**: organelle DNA comes from only one parent. Which parent depends on the organism: maternal in humans, paternal cpDNA in many conifers, mt⁺ cpDNA in *Chlamydomonas*. See [Organelle inheritance](organelle-inheritance/lec.qmd).

## Part 6: Gene regulation and development

### Prokaryotic regulation

**Attenuation**: control of transcription termination in a leader mRNA through alternative hairpins, as in the *trp* operon. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Cis-acting / trans-acting**: affecting only the DNA molecule it is on (a site), or acting on all copies through a diffusible product. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Constitutive mutant**: a mutant that expresses a gene with or without the inducer (e.g. *lacI*⁻, *lacO*ᶜ). See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Merodiploid**: a bacterium with a second copy of part of its genome, usually on an F′ plasmid. It is used to test dominance and cis/trans action. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Super-repressor (*lacI*ˢ)**: a repressor that cannot bind the inducer. It is uninducible and dominant in trans. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Polar mutation**: a nonsense mutation early in an operon gene that also lowers expression of the downstream genes on the same mRNA. It can wrongly appear to fail to complement them. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Promoter mutation (*P*⁻)**: a cis-acting change that stops RNA polymerase starting at a promoter. It is uninducible, but only the genes on its own DNA molecule are affected. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

**Repressible operon**: an operon that is on unless a small molecule (a corepressor, e.g. tryptophan) activates its repressor. The *trp* operon is the example. See [Prokaryotic regulation](prokaryotic-regulation-recap/lec.qmd).

### Eukaryotic regulation and epigenetics

**Barr body**: the condensed inactive X. A cell has (number of X − 1) of them. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Enhancer**: a cis-acting DNA element that raises transcription, often far from the gene and tissue-specific. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Epigenetics**: heritable changes in gene expression without a change in DNA sequence. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Genomic imprinting**: expression of only the maternal or only the paternal allele. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Motif**: the short, degenerate DNA sequence that a transcription factor binds. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Skewed X inactivation**: use of one X in at least 80% of the cells of a tissue (80:20 or more). See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Allele-specific expression**: the share of a gene's RNA made from each of its two alleles, measured with a SNP that tells them apart. Cis-acting variants make the shares unequal; trans-acting variants do not. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Hemi-methylated DNA**: a CpG site methylated on the old strand only, just after replication. DNMT1 methylates the new strand, and so copies the pattern. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Imprint resetting**: erasing the parental imprints in the germ line and setting new ones according to the parent's sex. The same allele can therefore be silent in one generation and active in the next. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Manifesting carrier**: a heterozygous woman who shows symptoms of an X-linked recessive disease, usually because of skewed X inactivation. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

**X inactivation**: random silencing of one X per cell in female mammals, inherited by the cell's descendants and started by *XIST*. See [Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics](eukaryotic-regulation/lec.qmd).

### RNA-mediated regulation

**Guide strand**: the strand of an siRNA or miRNA duplex that Argonaute keeps. For an siRNA it is the reverse complement of the target mRNA. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**lncRNA**: a non-coding transcript longer than 200 nt. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**miRNA family**: miRNAs that share a seed sequence and so target the same sites. Members can cover for each other. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Off-target effect**: knockdown of unintended mRNAs by an siRNA, mainly through miRNA-like pairing of its seed. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**microRNA (miRNA)**: a ~22-nt RNA from a hairpin in the genome that represses mRNAs through seed pairing. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**RNA interference (RNAi)**: silencing by siRNAs, made from double-stranded RNA, that guide cleavage of the matching mRNA. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Seed**: nucleotides 2–8 of a miRNA. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**Site type (8mer, 7mer-m8, 7mer-A1, 6mer)**: classes of miRNA target site, defined by pairing with seed nucleotides 2–8 or 2–7, and by whether there is an A opposite nucleotide 1. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

**siRNA**: a ~21-nt RNA made by Dicer from long double-stranded RNA. It pairs perfectly with one target. See [RNA-mediated regulation](rna-regulation/lec.qmd).

### Development and model organisms

**Balancer chromosome**: a chromosome with inversions, a dominant marker and a recessive lethal. It is used to keep mutations in stocks. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Denticle belt**: a band of small cuticle hooks on each segment of the *Drosophila* larva, used to read the phenotypes of segmentation mutants. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Gap / pair-rule / segment-polarity gene**: classes of segmentation gene. Their mutants lack a block of adjacent segments, every other segment, or part of each segment (replaced by a mirror image), respectively. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Homeotic transformation**: development of one body part with the identity of another, caused by Hox mutations. Loss of function gives a more anterior identity; ectopic gain gives a more posterior one. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Mosaic founder**: an F0 animal from a CRISPR-injected embryo whose cells carry different edits, or none. It is crossed to obtain offspring with one defined allele. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Reporter gene**: a gene with an easily detected product (e.g. *lacZ*) placed after a DNA fragment, to show where and when that fragment drives expression. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Forward / reverse genetics**: from phenotype to gene, or from gene to phenotype. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Hox genes / colinearity**: homeobox genes that give segments their identity. Their order on the chromosome matches the order of the body parts they specify. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).

**Maternal-effect gene**: a gene for which the embryo's phenotype depends on the mother's genotype. See [Development & model organisms](development-model-organisms/lec.qmd).



## Part 7: Cancer, populations and complex traits

### Cancer genetics

**Driver mutation**: a somatic mutation that gives a cell a growth advantage and is selected during tumour evolution. Contrast with a passenger mutation. See [Cancer genetics](cancer-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Loss of heterozygosity (LOH)**: loss of one allele of a heterozygous locus in a tumour, so nearby markers look homozygous in tumour DNA. See [Cancer genetics](cancer-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Mutator phenotype**: a raised mutation rate in a cell lineage, usually from loss of a DNA-repair gene. See [Cancer genetics](cancer-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Oncogene**: a mutated, overactive form of a gene that promotes cell division (the normal form is a proto-oncogene). It is a gain of function, so one mutant allele is enough: dominant at the cell level. See [Cancer genetics](cancer-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Tumour suppressor gene**: a gene whose product restrains division or repairs DNA. A cell becomes abnormal only when both alleles are lost: recessive at the cell level. See [Cancer genetics](cancer-genetics/lec.qmd).

**Two-hit hypothesis**: Knudson's model, in which a tumour arises when both alleles of a tumour suppressor are inactivated in one cell. In hereditary cases the first hit is inherited. See [Cancer genetics](cancer-genetics/lec.qmd).

### Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium

**Allele frequency**: the fraction of gene copies in a population that are a given allele; p = f(AA) + ½ f(Aa). See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

**de Finetti triangle**: a triangle in which each population is a point (q across, heterozygote frequency up). Populations in HWE lie on a parabola. See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

**Gene pool**: all the gametes of a population. Its allele frequencies equal *p* and *q*. See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

**Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)**: genotype frequencies p², 2pq and q². They are reached after one generation of random mating and stay constant without drift, selection, mutation or migration. See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

**Identical by descent**: two alleles that are copies of the same ancestral allele. See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

**Inbreeding coefficient (F)**: the probability that a person's two alleles are identical by descent. It is estimated as 1 − H~obs~/H~exp~. See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

**Wahlund effect**: a deficit of heterozygotes in a sample pooled from populations with different allele frequencies. See [Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium](hardy-weinberg/lec.qmd).

### Drift, selection, mutation, migration

**Effective population size (N~e~)**: the size of an ideal population that drifts as fast as the real one. It is usually much smaller than the census size. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Fixation**: an allele reaching frequency 1. For a neutral allele, the probability of fixation equals its current frequency. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Founder effect**: changes in allele frequencies because a new population starts from few individuals. A bottleneck has the same effect. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Gene flow (migration)**: movement of alleles between populations; Δp = m(p~M~ − p). See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Genetic drift**: random change in allele frequency due to the sampling of gene copies each generation. It is strongest in small populations. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Heterozygote advantage (overdominance)**: heterozygotes are fitter than both homozygotes, which keeps the allele at a stable intermediate frequency, as with HbS and malaria. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Mutation–selection balance**: an equilibrium in which new mutations replace the alleles removed by selection. For a recessive allele, q̂ ≈ √(μ/s). See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Relative fitness (w)**: the relative number of offspring left by a genotype. s is the selection coefficient and h the dominance of the fitness effect. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

**Wright–Fisher model**: a model of drift in which the next generation's 2N gene copies are drawn at random from the current one. See [Drift, selection, mutation, migration](drift-selection/lec.qmd).

### Complex traits, heritability and GWAS

**Bonferroni correction**: dividing the accepted error rate by the number of tests, e.g. 0.05/10⁶ = 5 × 10⁻⁸. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Breeder's equation**: *R* = *h*²*S*. The response to selection equals the narrow-sense heritability times the selection differential. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Broad-sense heritability (H²)**: V~G~/V~P~, the fraction of phenotypic variance due to all genetic differences. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Complex (quantitative) trait**: a continuously varying trait influenced by many loci and by the environment. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Genome-wide association study (GWAS)**: a test of association between a trait and each of very many SNPs in unrelated people. The significance threshold is 5 × 10⁻⁸. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Manhattan plot**: −log~10~ p of every SNP plotted against its position in the genome. Associated loci appear as towers. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Missing heritability**: the gap between heritability estimated from families and the variance explained by GWAS hits. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Narrow-sense heritability (h²)**: V~A~/V~P~, the fraction of phenotypic variance due to additive genetic variance. It equals the slope of offspring on midparent. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Odds ratio**: the odds of carrying the risk allele in cases divided by the odds in controls. It is the effect size in a case–control GWAS. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Polygenic score**: a person's sum of risk alleles, each weighted by its GWAS effect size. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Quantitative trait locus (QTL)**: a locus that affects a quantitative trait, mapped by linkage in crosses. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Selection differential (*S*)**: how far the mean of the selected parents lies above the population mean. See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

**Regression towards the mean**: offspring of extreme parents are on average less extreme, by the factor h². See [Complex traits, heritability & GWAS](complex-traits/lec.qmd).

## Ethics

**Autonomy**: respect for a person's own informed, voluntary choices. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Beneficence / non-maleficence**: the duty to do good, and the duty to avoid harm. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Direct-to-consumer (DTC) test**: a genetic test sold directly to the public, without a doctor. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Eugenics**: the attempt to "improve" a population by controlling reproduction. Galton coined the word in 1883. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Family letter**: a letter written by the clinic, which a patient passes on to relatives, about a genetic risk they share. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Gene drive**: an allele that copies itself onto the homologous chromosome, so that it reaches nearly all gametes instead of half. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Germline editing**: changing the DNA of an embryo or gametes so that the change is inherited. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Incidental / secondary finding**: a result unrelated to the reason for testing. An incidental finding turns up by chance; a secondary finding is looked for on purpose in actionable genes. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Informed consent**: voluntary agreement to a test or to research, given after understanding what it involves. It can be withdrawn. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Investigative genetic genealogy**: identifying the donor of crime-scene DNA through distant relatives in genealogy databases. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Justice (bioethics)**: fair distribution of the benefits, risks and costs of care and research. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**NIPT**: non-invasive prenatal testing, a screening test on cell-free fetal DNA in the mother's blood. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Predictive testing**: testing a healthy person for a variant that forecasts later disease, e.g. Huntington disease. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Re-identification**: recovering a person's identity from data with the names removed, e.g. surnames from Y-STRs. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).

**Right not to know**: a person's right to decline learning a genetic result about themselves. See [Ethics of genetic knowledge](ethics/lec.qmd).
